controls.label: Color + brightness
controls.qualification: The star's color, darker where TESS saw it dimmer (contrast drawn stronger) · September and October 2018, mapped in this project
controls.notes: BE Ceti in its own color, darker where its light in TESS's images of September and October 2018 says it was darker. As the star turned once in 7.76 days its light rose and fell by 2.1%. The contrast is drawn far stronger than it is, so the eye can see it: the darkest part gives 8% less light than the brightest, and is drawn as a much darker tone of the star's own hue; the Brightness map's scale has the measured values. The longitudes of the darker and brighter parts are measured. Their latitudes and shapes are not: they are the smoothest that reproduce the light. No change of color is drawn, because none is measured. Spots come and go within weeks or months: this is the star then. The darkening toward the edge is the Color dataset's limb law, drawn 1.5 times as strong.

controls.label: Brightness map
controls.qualification: Mapped in this project · TESS mission light curve, sector 3
controls.notes: Where the star's surface was darker and brighter in TESS sector 3, worked out in this project from how its light rose and fell by 2.1% as it turned once in 7.76 days. The light curve is the mission's own; Colman et al. (2024, AJ 167, 189) found the star's rotation in it, and starry finds the map that reproduces it at their period. The longitudes of the dark and bright regions are fixed by the data; their latitudes are not. The map is made at the tilt the page draws the star with, 65°.
controls.legendNote: Darker: dimmer than the star's mean surface; white: brighter. Black line: 65° S; the star never shows us what lies below it.

controls.label: Color
controls.qualification: Color of a blackbody at the star's temperature; darkening toward the edge from a model atmosphere. The disc itself is unresolved.
controls.notes: The color of a blackbody at the star's published temperature. The darkening toward the edge is the quadratic law Claret & Bloemen (2011), A&A 529, A75 compute from ATLAS model atmospheres for the Johnson V band at 5,837 K and log g 4.41 (u1 0.447, u2 0.267): a model, because no fit of this star's limb is used. The spin axis's direction on the sky is a display convention.

controls.label: Derived corona
controls.notes: No telescope has imaged this corona, and this is not a published result: it is derived here from the star's magnetic map by a standard method. Gas at rest is placed along the line where the field of the Dec 2017 map reverses, and the wind everywhere else. How much gas there is follows from three numbers. The star's X-ray output is measured (Freund et al. (2022), A&A 664, A105). Its coronal temperature, 4.7 million kelvin, is not measured: it is the temperature stars of this X-ray output have (Johnstone & Güdel (2015), A&A 578, A129). Its mass loss, 22 times the Sun's, is not measured either: it is what the X-ray output suggests (Wood et al. (2021), ApJ 915, 37). Stars with a measured wind lie within a factor of 5 of that relation, and one is 38 times below it. Drawn out to 4 stellar radii in the star's own color; at each distance brightness is proportional to density.
